REGULATION ON RECORD RETENTION
Chapter I
General provisions
Article 1. Definitions
In this Regulation:
(a) "record" means any information created or received by a provider in the course of its service;
(b) "provider" means a person that offers a hosted storage service to the public.
Article 2. Scope
This Regulation applies to providers established in the Republic.
Chapter II
Obligations
Article 3. Retention
1. A provider must retain each record for at least five years after its creation.
2. A provider must delete a record within thirty days after the end of the retention period referred to in paragraph 1.
3. A provider may retain a record longer where a court orders it.
Article 4. Disclosure
1. A provider must not disclose a record to a third party without the consent of the person to whom the record relates.
2. Paragraph 1 does not apply where disclosure is required by law.
Article 5. Notification
A provider must notify the supervisory authority of any loss of records within 72 hours of becoming aware of it.

# Acceptable Use Policy

## Purpose

This policy describes how company information systems may be used.

## Who this policy covers

This policy applies to all employees, contractors and temporary staff who use company systems.

## Requirements

Staff must lock their workstation whenever they leave it unattended.

Staff must report a suspected security incident to the security team within one hour of noticing it.

Staff must not install software that the IT department has not approved.

Staff may use company devices for limited personal purposes outside working hours.

## Exceptions

The security team may grant a written exception to the software installation rule where there is a documented business need.

## Background

The company operates a large number of laptops, desktop computers and mobile devices that are shared across several offices. Over the past years the security team has observed that most incidents begin with an unattended device or with software that was downloaded from an unknown source. These observations are summarised here so that readers understand why the requirements above exist. The summary is explanatory only and does not add any requirement beyond those listed in the Requirements section.

Unattended devices are a recurring concern because offices are open to visitors, cleaners and contractors at different times of day. A device that remains unlocked can be used by anyone who passes by, and actions taken from it are recorded under the name of the person who left it. The security team therefore considers screen locking to be one of the simplest and most effective protections that staff can apply, and it has configured devices to lock automatically after a short period of inactivity as an additional safeguard.

Software installed without review can contain hidden functions that collect information or open connections to external systems. In several past cases such software was offered for free and appeared harmless, but later updates changed its behaviour. The IT department maintains a catalogue of approved applications that have been reviewed for these risks, and the catalogue is updated regularly as new business needs are identified by teams across the company.

Prompt reporting matters because the damage caused by an incident usually grows with time. When the security team learns about a suspicious email, an unexpected login prompt or a lost device quickly, it can often contain the problem before information leaves the company. Reports that arrive days later frequently mean that the opportunity to limit the damage has already passed, which is why the policy asks for reports within a short period.

Personal use of company devices is tolerated within limits because staff sometimes need to complete small personal tasks during breaks. The limits exist because personal browsing increases exposure to unsafe websites and because company devices are not designed to store personal files. Staff who need extensive personal computing should use their own devices, which are not managed by the company and are not covered by company backups or support arrangements.

The company reviews this policy every year together with representatives of staff, the IT department and the security team. Suggestions for improvements are welcome at any time and are considered during the annual review. Changes are communicated through the usual internal channels and take effect on the date stated in the announcement, so that every team has enough time to adjust its procedures and train new colleagues.

This background section may be updated more often than the rest of the policy, because it reflects the current understanding of threats and practical experience. Such updates are editorial and do not change the meaning of the requirements, which can only be changed through the formal annual review described above.

MASTER SERVICES AGREEMENT
This Agreement is made between Alpha Hosting Ltd ("Supplier") and Beta Retail Ltd ("Customer").
Section 1. Definitions
"Services" means the hosting services described in Schedule A.
Section 2. Supplier obligations
The Supplier shall provide the Services with an availability of at least 99.5% in each calendar month.
The Supplier shall notify the Customer of any planned maintenance at least five business days in advance.
Section 3. Customer obligations
The Customer shall pay each undisputed invoice within thirty days of receipt.
The Customer may withhold payment of any amount it disputes in good faith.
Section 4. Term
This Agreement continues until terminated under Section 6.
Section 5. Data protection
"Personal Data" means information relating to an identified individual that the Supplier processes for the Customer.
The Supplier must process Personal Data only on the Customer's documented instructions.
Section 6. Termination
Either party may terminate this Agreement by giving ninety days' written notice.
Footnote 1: The Supplier must credit the Customer 5% of the monthly fee for each month in which availability falls below 99.5%.

STANDARD ON ELECTRONIC IDENTIFICATION
Article 1. Definitions
1. "Identity provider" means an entity that issues electronic identification means.
2. "Electronic identification means" means a material or immaterial unit containing person identification data that is used for authentication.
3. "Relying party" means a person that relies on electronic identification.
4. "Authentication" means an electronic process that enables the confirmation of the identity of a person.
5. "High assurance" means a level of assurance that provides a high degree of confidence in the claimed identity.
6. "Incident" means any event that compromises the security of electronic identification means.
7. "Qualified identity provider" means an identity provider that holds a valid certificate under this Standard.
8. A term defined in this Article has the same meaning throughout this Standard.
Article 2. Duties of identity providers
1. A qualified identity provider must offer authentication at high assurance.
2. An identity provider must notify each relying party of an incident within 24 hours.
Article 3. Relying parties
A relying party may refuse electronic identification means that do not provide high assurance.

RULES ON DATA TRANSFERS
Article 1. General rule
1. A controller must not transfer personal data outside the Union except as permitted by Article 2 or Article 3.
2. Paragraph 1 applies to every controller established in the Union.
Article 2. Adequacy
1. A controller may transfer personal data to a country that the Commission has declared adequate.
2. A transfer under paragraph 1 must be recorded in the register referred to in Article 4(2).
Article 3. Safeguards
1. In the absence of a decision under Article 2(1), a controller may transfer personal data if it applies the safeguards listed in point (a) or point (b) of paragraph 2.
2. The safeguards are:
(a) standard contractual clauses;
(b) binding corporate rules.
3. Point (b) of paragraph 2 is available only to controllers that belong to a group of undertakings.
Article 4. Records
1. Each controller must keep a register of transfers.
2. The register must contain the destination country and the legal basis of each transfer.
Article 5. Relationship with other law
This Regulation does not affect Article 5 of the Data Protection Act.
Article 6. Penalties
A breach of Article 9 is subject to penalties.

Guidance Note: Choosing Strong Passphrases

This guidance explains good practice for choosing passphrases. It does not create legal obligations and does not replace any applicable law or contract.

Many organizations find that longer passphrases are easier to remember than short complex passwords.

ApproachTypical effect
Four random wordsEasier to remember
Password managerFewer reused passwords

Readers may wish to discuss these options with their IT team.
